outline.chapter_title: Setting the Stage: FOIA, the Civil Service Reform Act, and the Office of Special Counsel
outline.description: Introduces the statutory architecture that frames the dispute: FOIA’s disclosure and disciplinary mechanisms, the Civil Service Reform Act’s investigative and enforcement provisions, and the roles of OSC and the MSPB.
subtopics: FOIA’s core disclosure right and private right of action
FOIA’s disciplinary trigger: 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) (court order + fee award + finding questioning arbitrariness/capriciousness)
The Civil Service Reform Act: purposes and structure
OSC’s mandates: 5 U.S.C. §§ 1214 (corrective action), 1215 (disciplinary action), 1216 (other misconduct, including arbitrary/capricious FOIA withholdings)
MSPB’s adjudicatory role and available remedies
How § 1216(c) cross-references §§ 1214 and 1215
Overlap and tensions between FOIA’s disciplinary mechanism and CSRA’s investigatory framework

outline.description: Covers the constitutional case-or-controversy requirement and the three irreducible elements: injury in fact, causation (traceability), and redressability, along with burdens at different litigation stages.
subtopics: Case-or-controversy and the role of standing (U.S. Const. art. III; Allen v. Wright)
Injury in fact: concrete, particularized, actual or imminent (Lujan; Spokeo; TransUnion)
Causation/traceability: linking injury to defendant’s conduct
Redressability: likelihood that a favorable court decision will remedy injury
Pleading-stage standards and plausibility (Food & Water Watch v. Vilsack)
No hypothetical jurisdiction (Steel Co. v. Citizens for a Better Environment)
Organizational standing versus representational standing (overview)

outline.chapter_title: Procedural Injury: Relaxed, Not Eliminated Requirements
outline.description: Explains the doctrine for standing based on violation of procedural rights, when courts relax imminence and redressability but still require a concrete interest affected by the violation.
subtopics: What counts as a procedural right and why it matters
Summers v. Earth Island Institute: no procedural right in vacuo
Center for Law & Education v. Department of Education; Florida Audubon Society v. Bentsen (en banc): relaxed but real requirements
Massachusetts v. EPA’s special solicitude (limitations and context)
Identifying the threatened concrete interest the procedure is designed to protect
Applying procedural-injury doctrine to investigative and notice provisions

outline.chapter_title: Informational Standing: When Denial of Information Is a Concrete Injury
outline.description: Analyzes the special strand of standing that arises when a statute itself confers a right to receive information and the plaintiff is denied that entitlement.
subtopics: Foundational cases: Public Citizen v. DOJ; FEC v. Akins; Zivotofsky
The entitlement requirement: the statute must mandate disclosure to the plaintiff
Distinguishing a right to information from an interest in governmental enforcement
The influence of Spokeo and TransUnion on concreteness in informational harms
OSC investigations and the absence of a statutory entitlement under 5 U.S.C. § 1216
Carson v. U.S. Office of Special Counsel: discretion to apply § 1214 procedures in § 1216 matters
FOIA’s distinct informational entitlement versus CSRA’s discretionary investigatory processes

outline.chapter_title: Independent Actors, Speculative Chains, and Redressability Limits
outline.description: Explores the barriers to standing when a plaintiff’s theory depends on choices by third parties or on agency enforcement discretion.
subtopics: Independent-actor doctrine and speculation concerns
FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine: redressability and independent choices
Haaland v. Brackeen: judgments bind parties, not nonparties persuaded by reasoning
Clapper v. Amnesty International and Simon v. Eastern Kentucky Welfare Rights (causal attenuation)
Hecate Energy LLC v. FERC: ‘very likely spur’ standard in multi-step causal chains
Heckler v. Chaney: enforcement discretion as a barrier to judicial compulsion
Applying these principles to multi-agency remedial paths (OSC → MSPB → agency compliance)

outline.chapter_title: The Road to the D.C. Circuit: Facts and Procedural History of AFL v. Greer
outline.description: Sets out the factual background of AFL’s FOIA request, its complaint to OSC, the district court’s rulings, and how standing became the central issue on appeal.
subtopics: AFL’s FOIA request to DOJ and the alleged ‘consent to search emails’ policy
Parallel FOIA litigation and ongoing record production
AFL’s petition to OSC invoking § 1216(a)(3) and OSC’s reliance on § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) predicates
District court’s conclusions: legal error on § 1216 scope; discretion under § 1216(c); remand without ordering investigation
OSC’s renewed refusal; entry of final judgment; appeal
De novo standard of review and the court’s sua sponte standing inquiry and supplemental briefing

outline.chapter_title: AFL v. Greer: The D.C. Circuit’s Standing Analysis
outline.description: Uses the opinion as the central teaching vehicle to apply standing doctrine to two asserted injuries—lack of FOIA records and lack of OSC investigative notices—and explains why both theories fail.
subtopics: Procedural right asserted under § 1216 and Summers’ prohibition on ‘procedural right in vacuo’
First theory (FOIA records): injury traceable to DOJ, not OSC; speculative multi-step causal chain (OSC → MSPB → DOJ)
Independent actors not before the court and enforcement discretion problems
Redressability focused on binding parties, not persuasive effects on nonparties
Second theory (OSC investigation information): absence of statutory entitlement under § 1216
Discretionary importation of § 1214’s notice provisions into § 1216 investigations (Carson and related authority)
Failure of injury-in-fact and redressability under informational-standing framing
Holding: lack of Article III standing; vacatur and remand to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction

outline.chapter_title: Merits Questions Deferred: The Scope of § 1216 and the FOIA Disciplinary Trigger
outline.description: Examines the unresolved merits issues flagged by the district court—how § 1216 interacts with § 552(a)(4)(F) and the extent of OSC’s duty to investigate—and why appellate jurisdictional limits foreclosed decision.
subtopics: Whether § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) limits or supplements § 1216(a)(3) (district court’s view versus OSC’s position)
The meaning of ‘shall…conduct an investigation’ in § 1216
§ 1216(c)’s reference to §§ 1214 and 1215: scope and discretion
APA § 706(1): compelling discrete, nondiscretionary action (Norton v. SUWA) and its potential application
Steel Co.’s bar on deciding merits without jurisdiction
Why the D.C. Circuit avoided these merits questions in light of standing

outline.chapter_title: Suing Oversight Agencies: Reviewability, Discretion, and Justiciability
outline.description: Places AFL v. Greer in the broader framework of attempts to compel agency investigations or prosecutions, and the doctrines that typically block such suits.
subtopics: Heckler v. Chaney and presumptive unreviewability of enforcement discretion
When ‘shall’ language overcomes discretion and when it does not
Carson v. OSC and other decisions on OSC’s procedural flexibility
Limits of mandamus and APA review in compelling investigations
Separation-of-powers concerns in judicial supervision of executive enforcement choices
Comparisons to FEC nonenforcement and Akins-type informational injuries

outline.chapter_title: Practical Guidance for FOIA Litigants and Watchdog Organizations
outline.description: Translates doctrine into strategy: how to structure claims and records to satisfy standing, when to target the disclosing agency rather than the oversight body, and how to trigger FOIA’s disciplinary mechanism.
subtopics: Target the source: suing the withholding agency under FOIA to obtain records
How to trigger § 552(a)(4)(F): court order, fees, and specific finding on arbitrariness/capriciousness
Avoiding speculative causal chains: seeking relief that directly binds the defendant
Building informational-standing claims: identifying clear statutory entitlements to information
Why ‘resource diversion’ and organizational standing require concrete, non-self-inflicted harms
Coordinating parallel FOIA and oversight strategies without undermining standing

outline.chapter_title: Comparative Notes, Circuit Trends, and Open Questions
outline.description: Surveys related decisions across circuits and identifies unresolved issues likely to recur in litigation over statutory investigations and informational injuries.
subtopics: D.C. Circuit’s trajectory on procedural and informational injuries post-Spokeo/TransUnion
Sixth Circuit’s approach in Carson and implications for OSC practices
Tensions between Akins-style informational standing and attempts to compel enforcement
Potential circuit splits on when ‘shall investigate’ creates judicially enforceable duties
Unresolved questions about § 1216’s mandatory scope and the use of § 1214 procedures
Prospects for Supreme Court clarification on informational standing boundaries

outline.chapter_title: Synthesis and Significance: AFL v. Greer in the Standing Canon
outline.description: Assesses how the decision refines standing doctrine at the intersection of procedural and informational injuries and what it signals for future suits seeking to spur executive branch investigations.
subtopics: Reaffirmation that procedural rights require a concrete, affected interest
Clarification that not every ‘shall investigate’ yields an informational entitlement
Strengthening of redressability limits where multiple independent actors intervene
Boundary-setting for watchdog litigation against enforcement agencies
Doctrinal integration with Summers, Akins/Public Citizen, Chaney, and Brackeen
Legislative design lessons: crafting enforceable entitlements versus discretionary oversight
